reasoning.Student A:
My goal is to be matched to the school I like the most from the set of schools that would accept me. My preferences are w > y > z > x.

School w has priority 1 for me, so it is very likely I can get in.
School y has priority 1 for me, so it is very likely I can get in.
School z has priority 2 for me.
School x has priority 2 for me.

Since w and y are my top choices and I have priority 1 at both, I should rank them first. I prefer w > y, so I rank w first.

Now I need to decide the order of z and x. I prefer z > x. Since I have priority 2 at both, it is possible I get neither. However, the ranking does not change which schools are obtainable. So I should rank the schools in order of my preference.

Therefore, my ranking should be w > y > z > x.
reasoning.Student B:
My goal is to be matched with my most preferred school from the "obtainable set". The obtainable set is determined by the school priorities. I want to figure out which schools are potentially obtainable and then rank them according to my preferences.

School w: My priority is 2.
School x: My priority is 1.
School y: My priority is 2.
School z: My priority is 1.

Since my priority at x and z are both 1, these schools are very likely to be in my obtainable set. My priority at w and y are both 2, so they may or may not be in my obtainable set, depending on how many other students have priority 1 at those schools.

My preferences are y > w > z > x.

Scenario 1: Both y and w are obtainable.
In this case, I should rank y > w > z > x to get my most preferred school y.

Scenario 2: Only y is obtainable.
I should rank y first. The rest of the ranking doesn't matter as long as y is first. y > w > z > x.

Scenario 3: Only w is obtainable.
I should rank w first. The rest of the ranking doesn't matter as long as w is first. y > w > z > x will still result in w.

Scenario 4: Neither y nor w are obtainable.
Then I will be matched to either z or x. Since I prefer z > x, I want to ensure that if only z is obtainable, I get z. So I should rank z higher than x. y > w > z > x will still result in z.

In all scenarios, ranking y > w > z > x will give me the best possible outcome.
reasoning.Student C:
My goal is to maximize my chances of attending my most preferred school, y. Since my outcome is determined by my priorities at each school, and not my ranking, I want to apply to my favorite schools first. This is because if I get into my favorite school, I will attend it.

My preference is y > w > z > x. My priorities are: w: 3, x: 3, y: 4, z: 4.

I should rank my schools in order of preference: y > w > z > x. This is because, regardless of the ranking, I will be matched to my most preferred school within my "obtainable set". Therefore, ranking according to my true preferences will guarantee that I get my best possible outcome.

I should rank the schools in my true preference order to ensure I get my best possible match *if* I get into any school.

School y is my top choice and I have a priority rank of 3 there. School z is my second choice and I have a priority rank of 3 there as well. School w is my third choice and I have a priority rank of 4 there. School x is my last choice and I have a priority rank of 4 there.

Given the information that most applicants favor y > x > w > z, this suggests that y will be very competitive. However, my priority at y and z is better than at w and x. Thus, I should rank the schools in my true preference order.
